title: Unbounded number of uploaded file parts allows resource-exhaustion DoS
impact: A single multipart request containing a very large number of small file parts causes creation of a correspondingly large number of temporary files and handler invocations, exhausting file descriptors, inodes, disk space, and CPU on the server, resulting in denial of service. There is no default Django-level cap on the number of file parts (no DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FILES setting exists in this version).
description: The multipart parser gates FIELD parts against settings.DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS, but the FILE branch (item_type == FILE) has no per-request limit on the number of file parts; each part invokes handler.new_file(), which for the default TemporaryFileUploadHandler creates a new on-disk temporary file. An unauthenticated attacker controls the number of parts via the request body.
exploit_scenario: An attacker POSTs multipart/form-data to any view that reads request.POST/request.FILES (or triggers upload parsing). The body contains hundreds of thousands of minimal file parts (each ~70 bytes: a Content-Disposition with a filename and empty content). The parser calls new_file() for every part, spawning that many NamedTemporaryFile handles and consuming server resources until file descriptors/inodes/disk are exhausted.
preconditions: A request path that causes multipart parsing (any view accessing request.POST or request.FILES on a POST, or middleware doing so)
No front-end proxy imposing a strict request-body-size or part-count limit
category: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
recommendation: Introduce and enforce a DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FILES limit in the FILE branch analogous to the DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS check, raising TooManyFilesSent when exceeded (this is the fix later shipped as CVE-2023-24580 mitigation).

title: Multipart filename sanitized before HTML-unescape, allowing path separators to be reintroduced
impact: The parser emits file names such as '../../../x' or '..' from crafted/HTML-encoded Content-Disposition filenames. This is the weakness class behind CVE-2021-31542 (this snapshot dated 2021-04-06 predates the May 2021 fix that reordered sanitization and added validate_file_name). Whether traversal reaches the filesystem depends on downstream consumers; django/core/files/uploadedfile.py re-applies os.path.basename (neutralizing embedded '/'), but a name of exactly '..' still passes through both basename calls and can cause directory traversal when the application saves the file under uploaded_file.name via Storage.
description: The uploaded filename from the attacker-controlled Content-Disposition header is passed through os.path.basename() (line 215) BEFORE html.unescape() (line 217); html.unescape can reintroduce '/' (e.g. '/') and path components after basename has already run, so the value handed to upload handlers can contain traversal sequences.
exploit_scenario: An attacker submits multipart/form-data with Content-Disposition filename='..' (or an HTML-encoded separator sequence). The parser produces file_name='..', which survives UploadedFile._set_name's basename. An application that saves the upload using the provided name (a common pattern) then writes/overwrites a path one directory above the intended upload location.
preconditions: Application saves uploaded files using the client-supplied name (uploaded_file.name) via a Storage backend
Downstream Storage does not independently reject '..'/path components (out of scope for django/http)
recommendation: Apply html.unescape and force_str before os.path.basename, and explicitly reject names that are '.', '..', or contain path separators (as done by the later validate_file_name fix).

title: Sibling consumer not covered by F2's patch: _set_name
impact: The parser emits file names such as '../../../x' or '..' from crafted/HTML-encoded Content-Disposition filenames. This is the weakness class behind CVE-2021-31542 (this snapshot dated 2021-04-06 predates the May 2021 fix that reordered sanitization and added validate_file_name). Whether traversal reaches the filesystem depends on downstream consumers; django/core/files/uploadedfile.py re-applies os.path.basename (neutralizing embedded '/'), but a name of exactly '..' still passes through both basename calls and can cause directory traversal when the application saves the file under uploaded_file.name via Storage.
description: The value protected by F2 also reaches _set_name in django/core/files/uploadedfile.py without the guard the patch introduces. This setter still runs os.path.basename() on the name assigned to UploadedFile.name, independent of the new sanitize_file_name gate. It's not in the scope of the F2 fix and doesn't unescape HTML entities, but since new_file() in TemporaryFileUploadHandler/InMemoryUploadedFile constructs UploadedFile with self.file_name (already sanitized), this consumer receives an already-sanitized value in the normal flow. However, if any other caller passes an unsanitized, HTML-encoded name directly to UploadedFile(name=...), basename() would run pre-unescape here, but this is outside the file_name flow controlled by the guard and not shown to be reachable with raw header data in the excerpts.
exploit_scenario: As for F2, via _set_name instead of the patched site.
preconditions: Application saves uploaded files using the client-supplied name (uploaded_file.name) via a Storage backend
Downstream Storage does not independently reject '..'/path components (out of scope for django/http)
recommendation: Apply the same guard as F2 at this consumer, or route the value through the patched path. Not patched here: run Suggest patches on this finding.
